title: Impact of substrate pH and micronutrient fertility rates on Cannabis sativa
publisher: Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy
supportedClaims: In a controlled peat-perlite experiment, industrial hemp shoot dry weight was lower at substrate pH 3.0 and 4.0 than at pH 5.0 through 7.0; plant diameter was smaller at pH 3.0, while mean plant height did not differ across that pH range.
Visible root-tip counts in Cannabis sativa Baox mini-rhizotrons were lowest at both measured extremes, pH 3.1 and 7.1, by 21 days after planting, while counts at pH 3.7 through 5.9 were similar.
Termination EC was higher at pH 3.0 and 7.0 than at intermediate pH values in the first experiment, so pH response cannot be interpreted without the accompanying salt and fertility context.

Lower pH increased several leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations, but normal micronutrient supply did not produce a universal toxicity phenotype; the authors concluded that Cannabis growth was inhibited below pH 5.0 and recommended a greenhouse substrate range of 5.5 to 6.5 for the systems evaluated.

With fourfold micronutrients at target pH 3.8, Sweetened developed lower-foliage tip bronzing that advanced to necrosis, inward spread, and chlorosis, whereas Cherry Wine did not show the same response, demonstrating cultivar- and fertility-dependent appearance.

The experiments evaluated peat-based greenhouse substrates and three cultivars; their pH values, timing, tissue concentrations, and symptom expression are treatment-specific and do not establish universal soil, coco, rockwool, or hydroponic thresholds.

title: Evaluating herbicide tolerance of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: In a randomized greenhouse pre-emergence screen using Cannabis sativa cultivar Felina 32, clomazone at 1.4 kg active ingredient per hectare produced only two surviving plants per pot, 8 cm mean plant height, and 0.6 g mean biomass at eight weeks, versus seven plants, 49 cm, and 13.5 g in the untreated check.

Across the greenhouse screen, clomazone was among treatments that reduced stand count 43–71%, height 47–84%, and biomass 73–96% relative to the untreated check; the paper groups clomazone and norflurazon as highly injurious pigment inhibitors.

Clomazone was screened pre-emergence in the greenhouse but was not advanced into the field study, so the experiment supports severe hemp sensitivity under its tested rate and conditions rather than a universal field threshold or a visual diagnosis.
The authors reported that hemp responses varied across environments, years, and cultivars for tested herbicides and called for corroboration before commercial recommendations.

title: Accumulation of somatic mutations leads to genetic mosaicism in cannabis
publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: Deep whole-genome sequencing of top, middle, and bottom samples from one 1.5-year-old Cannabis mother plant detected many variants unique to individual canopy samples, demonstrating within-plant genetic mosaicism in that plant.
The study examined a single mother plant and did not validate a visible leaf-sector pattern as a diagnostic marker of somatic mutation, heritability, or clonal stability.

title: Bacterial leaf spot of hemp caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Japan
publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Phytopathological Society of Japan
supportedClaims: The cannabis-specific Japanese report described leaf lesions with necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter and yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide.
Pathological, physiological, and genetic characterization linked the Japanese causal bacterium to the organism historically named Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Romania.

title: Temperature response of photosynthesis in different drug and fiber varieties of Cannabis sativa L.
organization: Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants (Chandra et al.)
publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Prof. H. S. Srivastava Foundation for Science and Society
supportedClaims: Across three drug-type and four fiber-type Cannabis varieties measured from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius, photosynthetic optima varied by variety from about 25 to 35 degrees Celsius.

Dark respiration approximately doubled from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius in all tested varieties, while photosynthesis, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency showed variety-dependent responses.
The experiment measured gas exchange rather than a validated visible heat-injury syndrome, so its temperature values must not be used as universal image-label thresholds.

title: High air temperature reduces plant specialized metabolite yield in medical cannabis, and has genotype-specific effects on inflorescence dry matter production
organization: Environmental and Experimental Botany (Holweg et al.)
supportedClaims: In controlled short-day production, plants of two medical Cannabis genotypes were compared at 25/21 and 31/27 degrees Celsius day/night temperatures and at PPFDs of 600, 900, and 1,200 micromoles per square metre per second.

The higher-temperature treatment reduced total cannabinoid concentration in both genotypes but reduced inflorescence dry matter only in Harmony CBD, demonstrating a genotype-specific production response.

High temperature produced abnormal new inflorescence clusters on top of older inflorescences and disrupted normal maturation; this flowering morphology is treatment-associated but is not a universal image-only heat threshold.

title: Physiological and morphological responses of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) to water deficit
organization: Industrial Crops and Products (Gill et al.)
supportedClaims: An 85-day greenhouse experiment on industrial hemp cultivar Black Label compared moderate and extreme water deficit with a control and measured morphological, physiological, and biochemical responses.

Water deficit reduced total biomass and total seed yield, reduced stomatal opening and transpiration, increased water-use efficiency and proline accumulation, and still allowed plants to survive and produce filled seed under the tested conditions.

These single-cultivar endpoint responses support drought as a growth and yield stress but do not validate a universal visible severity scale, mortality expectation, or cannabinoid-production response for other Cannabis genotypes and stages.
The article is marked in copyright by its institutional repository; no image, figure, or video is indexed or copied as reusable media.

title: Dioecious hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) plants do not express significant sexually dimorphic morphology in the seedling stage
supportedClaims: In a study of 112 dioecious hemp plants, seedling morphology did not consistently distinguish male, female, and co-sexual plants across cultivars.
The researchers assigned expressed sex after flowering from floral morphology; 10 plants were co-sexual, defined as predominantly female flowering with at least one male flower.
Male flowers on co-sexual plants may be concealed within dense female inflorescences and may not be found until after pollen release, so one early view is not an adequate exclusion check.

title: Pot size matters: a meta-analysis of the effects of rooting volume on plant growth
supportedClaims: A meta-analysis of 65 plant studies found that doubling pot size increased biomass by 43% on average and that reduced growth in smaller pots was associated mainly with lower photosynthesis per unit leaf area.

The analysis establishes that rooting volume can materially alter plant growth, but it is not Cannabis-specific and does not validate a universal Cannabis container size, root-density threshold, visual symptom, or field diagnosis.

The authors caution that appropriate pot size depends on plant size; the paper's experimental biomass-per-volume proposal is research-design guidance and is not a diagnostic threshold for cultivated Cannabis.

title: Seeing double on Cannabis: Haploids and heteroploids of Bipolaris gigantea on hemp and other dicots
publisher: Taylor & Francis on behalf of the Mycological Society of America
supportedClaims: The study examined Bipolaris gigantea isolates from hemp leaf-spot lesions and nearby weeds collected across 11 Kentucky counties.
Twenty-three isolates were analyzed by multilocus phylogenetics and seven were also whole-genome sequenced, revealing multiple genotypes and both haploid and apparently heteroploid isolates.
Haploid and heteroploid isolates caused similar disease on hemp, so lesion appearance cannot resolve ploidy, genotype, or the source host.

Species- and genotype-level labels therefore require lesion-linked laboratory evidence; a symptom photograph or single recovered isolate cannot establish population structure or transmission direction.

title: Root and crown rot pathogens causing wilt symptoms on field-grown marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) plants
supportedClaims: Affected field-grown Cannabis plants showed general or one-sided yellowing, rapid wilting, and collapse, with dark sunken crown lesions and internal discoloration extending upward from the root/crown zone.

Fusarium oxysporum, F. brachygibbosum, F. solani, F. equiseti, and Pythium aphanidermatum were recovered from affected tissues; pathogenicity work demonstrates that visual wilt alone does not identify one causal species.
Darkened or necrotic roots, crown rot, and reddish-brown internal decay are more discriminating observations than general canopy yellowing.

title: Several Pythium species cause crown and root rot on cannabis plants grown under commercial greenhouse conditions
organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across 140 diseased plants sampled from seven licensed commercial greenhouses in British Columbia during 2018 and 2019, the authors associated several Pythium or Globisporangium species with crown rot, root decay, wilting, and plant death; mother, vegetative, and flowering plants across 15 strains were affected.

Recovered isolates caused root browning, decay, and stunting in Cannabis grown in coco coir–perlite, but symptom rate and severity varied among isolates; visual appearance therefore cannot resolve the causal species.
Root wounding and prolonged saturation increased disease in the reported experiments, but these are risk modifiers rather than image-level proof of Pythium disease.
The study documented damping-off in rooted cuttings and secondary canopy yellowing, necrosis, defoliation, wilting, and death, alongside crown rot and internal pith browning or blackening.

title: Pathogenicity of seedborne Alternaria and Stemphylium species and stem-infecting Neofusicoccum and Lasiodiplodia species to cannabis (Cannabis sativa L., marijuana) plants
supportedClaims: Alternaria alternata was recovered from Cannabis inflorescences and surface-sterilized hemp seed in Canadian production material, extending the diagnostic context beyond leaf lesions alone.
The study confirmed pathogenicity of recovered fungi by inoculating Cannabis leaves, stems, buds, rooted cuttings, and mature plants; disease ratings varied with tissue type and pathogen.
Alternaria, Stemphylium, Neofusicoccum, and Lasiodiplodia were evaluated in the same work, so a lesion or blight photograph cannot assign Alternaria without plant-linked organism evidence.
The article is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no figure was admitted as media because a stable item-level original asset URL and panel-resolved Cannabis Alternaria label were not verified in this review.

title: Symptomology, Prevalence, and Impact of Hop Latent Viroid on Greenhouse-Grown Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plants in Canada
organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse production samples, symptom expression varied with growth stage and genotype: stock and vegetative plants ranged from asymptomatic to mild leaf curl and mottling, while flowering plants could show extreme stunting and reduced inflorescence development.

HLVd was detected in upper, middle, and lower canopy leaves and in roots, but its distribution varied among plant tissues and genotypes; one leaf position is therefore not a universal sampling rule or a reliable negative control.

Under the study conditions, infected flowering plants showed genotype-dependent reductions of 12–42% in inflorescence stem length, fresh weight, and plant height compared with noninfected plants, and diseased inflorescences had lower THC and terpene levels.

Glandular trichomes on affected plants had shorter stalks and smaller heads and appeared shrivelled after inflorescences were dried; these group-level measurements do not make sparse trichomes or reduced resin a visually specific HLVd sign.
The article is CC BY 4.0, but its stage, genotype, and tissue comparisons must remain source-grouped and laboratory-bounded if individual figures are later evaluated for training.

title: Physiological screening for drought-tolerance traits among hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) cultivars in controlled environments and in field
organization: Journal of Crop Improvement (Sheldon et al.)
supportedClaims: Progressive soil-drying trials found substantial cultivar differences in the fraction-of-transpirable-soil-water point at which hemp transpiration declined; five of thirteen cultivars closed stomata comparatively early.
A separate high-VPD screen found cultivar-specific limited-transpiration responses, with fitted VPD breakpoints ranging from 1.2 to 2.6 kPa among four responsive cultivars.

In a rainfed field comparison of six cultivars, wilting scores and relative water content differed among cultivars; Ha3ze, Carolina, and topped T1 had the lowest wilting scores during the reported midday observation period.
Wilting posture therefore depends on genotype, soil drying, atmospheric demand, observation time, and acclimation; the study does not establish one image-only drought threshold for Cannabis.
The publisher PDF and its plots do not provide verified reusable item-level media rights for this dataset, so no figure or frame is indexed as training or display media.

title: Assessing the impact of piercing-sucking pests on greenhouse-grown industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Broad mites are recognized among the most significant piercing-sucking pests of greenhouse-grown hemp.

Piercing-sucking pest injury in hemp can overlap visually with cupping, yellowing, leaf loss, and reduced reproductive performance, so pest presence must be confirmed rather than inferred from canopy symptoms.

title: Cannabinoids function in defense against chewing herbivores in Cannabis sativa L.
publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of Nanjing Agricultural University
supportedClaims: In a controlled detached-leaf assay, single Trichoplusia ni neonates fed for six days on leaves from 12 cutting-propagated Cannabis sativa F2 genotypes: six CBD-dominant and six cannabinoid-free genotypes.
Trichoplusia ni larvae consumed more leaf area and reached greater final mass on cannabinoid-free Cannabis genotypes than on CBD-dominant genotypes in the detached-leaf assay.

The detached-leaf assay establishes that Trichoplusia ni can consume Cannabis leaf tissue, but the species was not observed in the study field plots and was used as a model generalist herbivore; the experiment therefore does not establish field prevalence, canopy distribution, progression, injury thresholds, or yield loss on hemp.

Larvae in the detached-leaf assay were more often observed on the abaxial surface of cannabinoid-free leaves, but this laboratory behavior must not be converted into a universal field location or diagnostic threshold.

Cannabinoid chemotype, genotype, and trichome morphology affected feeding context, so severity or susceptibility observed in this limited F2 population must not be generalized across Cannabis cultivars.

title: Novel Approach to Tally Aculops cannabicola (Acari: Eriophyidae) Using Photographs of Hemp Leaves
organization: Journal of Economic Entomology (Falcon-Brindis et al.)
publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Hemp russet mites are approximately 160–210 micrometres long and are easily missed with standard low-power hand lenses.
Image-based counts require microscope photographs of multiple leaflet sections; ordinary whole-plant photographs cannot confirm the pest.
Feeding is associated with chlorosis, stunting, brittle leaf breakage, and reduced flower-bud size or resin production at high populations.

title: Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid (Hemiptera: Aphididae) in North America
publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Indoor Cannabis sativa has emerged as a common North American host of rice root aphid, Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale.

The authors observed rice root aphid in Cannabis soil, aeroponic, coconut-coir, and rockwool systems, but had not found it in outdoor hemp plantings; the outdoor evidence gap must not be converted into an absence claim.

In indoor Cannabis the aphid is almost entirely root-associated; alate females can emerge from soil especially during flowering and near maturity, colonize new plants, and produce young on stems or foliage before most offspring migrate downward.
Dead alates trapped on upper-leaf hairs can be an early facility-level cue, but a sticky-card or canopy alate is not plant-linked confirmation of a root colony.
Heavy Cannabis infestations were associated with generalized decline, slower growth, and possible lower-leaf off-coloration, none of which is unique to rice root aphid.
The article explicitly states that a Cannabis association with increased pathogen susceptibility still requires confirmation; root discoloration or decay must therefore be diagnosed independently.

title: Spotted cucumber beetle/southern corn rootworm: profile of a polyphagous native pest
publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Adults are 5.2 to 7.5 mm long, yellow to yellowish green, with a black head, dark antennae longer than half the body, and 12 black elytral spots; eastern and western subspecies differ in leg and abdominal coloration.

Larvae are soil-dwelling, yellowish-white and wormlike with brown legs and dark head, thoracic, and anal plates, but their economically important root feeding is documented on non-Cannabis crops rather than hemp.
The species feeds on more than 200 plant species and can occur on hemp, but damage on many hosts is cosmetic or inconsequential and action thresholds are not well developed.
Adults are mobile and populations can increase into late summer, but geography, subspecies, climate, host, and crop context prevent a universal Cannabis timing or severity rule.
General species biology and non-Cannabis injury examples are identification and transfer context only; they do not prove that a photographed hemp root, leaf, or flower was injured by this beetle.

title: Profile of the Dectes stem borer (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae) in sunflower and soybean
organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Varenhorst et al.)
publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: In sunflower and soybean, adults are dark brown to black under dense light-gray pubescence, measure 6 to 11 mm long, and normally hold curved antennae forward with the tips directed downward.
Larvae are legless, have an orange-red head capsule and accordion-like body tapering toward the rear, and range from approximately 1.5 mm in early instars to 12.5 mm when mature.

The reviewed non-Cannabis sequence is egg deposition in petiole tissue, larval pith tunneling, movement toward the stem base, internal girdling, a frass-plugged overwintering chamber, and possible lodging; Cannabis timing and frequencies have not been established.
Adult abundance does not reliably predict the percentage of infested stems, and internal feeding requires stem dissection for confirmation.
Dectes adults may be confused with ashgray blister beetle, while historical Dectes texanus versus Dectes sayi species boundaries contain morphological ambiguity that may require molecular analysis.
Management timing and efficacy vary by geography and season, and the review does not establish a hemp economic threshold or a hemp-labeled treatment.

title: Developing Insect Pest Management Systems for Hemp in the United States: A Work in Progress
organization: Journal of Integrated Pest Management (Cranshaw et al.)
publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: The southern corn rootworm or spotted cucumber beetle, Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi, was frequently observed on hemp east of the Rockies; adults fed on leaves but appeared to prefer flowers.

Lygus species were among the insects most commonly encountered on hemp, at least tarnished plant bug and pale legume bug bred on the crop, and Lygus lineolaris occurred from emergence to harvest in Virginia observations.
The 2019 hemp synthesis reported that no visible leaf injury by Lygus species had yet been observed, while seed-feeding injury potential remained unclear.

Lygus numbers could be higher after flowering, but flower-bud abscission, seed abortion, and seed deformity were effects known from other crops and hemp data were then absent to establish significance for seed production or quality.
Japanese beetle was observed on hemp east of the Mississippi as a highly visible, potentially significant defoliator that also feeds readily on hemp flowers; Figure 4 documents an adult on hemp.

Across the broader hemp defoliator complex, serious defoliation had only rarely been observed and experiments were still needed to connect defoliation with seed, fiber, cannabinoid, and biomass outcomes.

The 2019 profile was an early synthesis based mainly on Colorado, Virginia, and Tennessee observations through the end of 2018, so it does not establish a universal hemp action threshold or cultivar response.

Onion thrips was the species commonly found on hemp foliage in eastern Colorado and could cause serious foliage damage during indoor production, while outdoor populations generally failed to reach damaging levels.
Western flower thrips was also identified on Colorado hemp but was associated mainly with flowers and pollen; tobacco thrips was reported on young plants in an earlier Mississippi survey.
Thrips on hemp remained incompletely characterized, so visual injury cannot safely assign species or predict economic impact without organism sampling and production context.

title: Rhizoctonia Sore Shin and Root Rot
supportedClaims: The Cannabis-specific compendium identifies sore shin and root rot as a disease caused by the soil fungus Rhizoctonia solani.

The chapter describes Rhizoctonia sore shin and root rot as the first recorded seedling disease of Cannabis in Ukraine; this is historical crop evidence and does not establish current prevalence, cultivar response, or a universal seedling-onset rule.

The chapter is Cannabis-specific and peer reviewed, but the abstract alone does not support assigning Rhizoctonia from canopy wilt, lesion color, production environment, or an image without organism-linked evidence.

title: Root-Knot Nematodes
supportedClaims: Infection of hemp by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) is established, although the extent of Cannabis yield loss is not well quantified.
Organism confirmation and root signs are required; above-ground stunting or chlorosis alone is nonspecific.

title: First Report of Powdery Mildew Caused by Golovinomyces spadiceus on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: The Kentucky report identified a powdery mildew on industrial hemp as Golovinomyces spadiceus using fungal morphology and ITS plus 28S sequence evidence.
The historical G. spadiceus name in this report is now generally treated within the amended G. ambrosiae concept; the DOI must not be cited as though its original title named G. ambrosiae.

title: First Report of Sclerotinia Crown Rot Caused by Sclerotinia minor on Hemp
supportedClaims: Sclerotinia minor caused crown rot on field-grown hemp; foliage wilted and dried while the soil-contact crown developed white-to-gray mycelium and small irregular black sclerotia.
The crown-centered S. minor disease overlaps white-mold syndromes but requires organism-level confirmation rather than a canopy-only label.

title: First Report of ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii’ Associated with a Witches’ Broom Disease in Cannabis sativa in Nevada, U.S.A
supportedClaims: Symptomatic Nevada cannabis had leaf curling, mottling, chlorosis, witches’ broom, stunting, and shortened nodes.
Upper leaf surfaces showed vein-bounded green islands while lower surfaces showed interveinal discoloration with a pale pustule-like appearance.

Phytoplasma was detected from petioles of the most symptomatic leaves by 23S rRNA real-time PCR; nested 16S rRNA PCR, Sanger sequencing, BLASTn, and iPhyClassifier analysis supported identification near Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii.

title: First Report of Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Cercospora leaf spot began on older lower-canopy hemp leaves as small yellow flecks and progressed to round 2 to 6 mm lesions with tan-to-white centers, dark brown-to-purplish borders, and yellow halos.
Melanized conidiophores could become visible in lesion centers before centers disintegrated.
Whole-plant inoculation reproduced similar symptoms and the fungus was recovered again, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.

title: First Report of Leaf Spot on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Alternaria alternata in China
supportedClaims: Industrial hemp leaf spots began as small spots and developed into brown irregular lesions with light yellow halos; lesion centers could perforate as disease advanced.
The isolate was identified as Alternaria alternata by morphology and multilocus molecular evidence, and inoculated healthy hemp developed similar lesions while controls remained asymptomatic.
Re-isolation from inoculated plants fulfilled Koch postulates, so the record supports an organism-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot diagnosis rather than visual similarity alone.

title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in California
supportedClaims: Greenhouse medical Cannabis with Pythium myriotylum root rot showed stunting, chlorosis, senescence, reduced root mass and root-hair density, and necrotic root lesions.
The Cannabis-specific phenotype does not make canopy appearance species-specific.

title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Causing Crown and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot has been confirmed in indoor Cannabis grown in rockwool across multiple cultivars in Florida.
Species occurrence across production systems supports retaining a Pythium complex label unless laboratory evidence resolves species.

title: First Report of Serratia marcescens Causing a Leaf Spot Disease on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: Greenhouse-grown hemp developed small dark-brown 1–3 mm vein-limited angular lesions on leaves, stems, and flower parts; lesions coalesced into larger necrotic regions and red bacterial ooze was observed.
Serratia marcescens was supported by colony/microscopic traits and 16S rRNA plus rpoB sequence evidence.
Inoculated hemp developed similar lesions, controls remained symptomless, and the organism was reisolated, providing pathogenicity evidence rather than visual association alone.

The original observation and pathogenicity work were greenhouse-bound and included Cannabis sativa cultivar Carmagnola, so they do not establish universal field, cultivar, age, severity, or timing labels.

title: Curly Top Disease of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California Is Caused by Mild-Type Strains of Beet curly top virus Often in Mixed Infection
supportedClaims: California hemp plants with curly-top-like disease were characteristically stunted and bushy with distorted, upward-curled, yellowed leaves.
A multiplex PCR detected Beet curly top virus in 89% of hemp samples with curly-top-like symptoms, while other symptom types had low BCTV incidence and were associated with other factors.
An infectious BCTV-CO clone reproduced curly-top-like symptoms in hemp, fulfilling Koch’s postulates; mixed BCTV strain infections also occurred.

title: Detection and Quantification of Latent Infection by Fusarium graminearum, Causal Agent of Fusarium Head Blight on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Fields in Kentucky
supportedClaims: A multi-site hemp field study used species-specific qPCR to detect and quantify F. graminearum in asymptomatic and symptomatic tissues.
Latent infection occurred before visible disease and infection was more prominent during flowering, so absence of visible blight cannot exclude infection and image-only confirmation is unsafe.

title: First Report of White Root Rot of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Dematophora necatrix in Campania Region (Southern Italy)
supportedClaims: Affected hemp developed yellowing, apical wilt, root rot, white mycelium covering roots, and fan-like mycelium beneath root bark before death.
In the reported field, death generally occurred within two to three weeks after first symptoms and about 10% of plants were affected.
Inoculated hemp reproduced chlorosis, apical wilt, and death while controls remained healthy; the fungus was reisolated and confirmed by morphology and molecular analysis.
Root signs and laboratory confirmation are required because canopy yellowing and wilt overlap many Cannabis root-zone disorders.

title: First Report of Pythium myriotylum Causing Damping off and Root Rot in Cannabis sativa in Florida
supportedClaims: Pythium myriotylum was confirmed causing damping-off and root rot in indoor Cannabis cuttings from five cultivars in Florida.
The expanded cultivar evidence supports propagation-stage scouting and reinforces that Pythium disease can occur before a mature-plant canopy syndrome is available.

title: First Report of Exserohilum rostratum Causing Foliar Blight of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: During the 2017 and 2018 North Carolina growing seasons, several industrial-hemp cultivars grown for fiber, seed, and flower showed foliar, stem, and floral blight, establishing a multi-organ Cannabis disease context rather than a generic non-host transfer.
Compatible hemp lesions were round and brown to black with dark margins and contained abundant conidia; lesion appearance alone was not the basis for the organism label.
Fungal morphology together with ITS1 and RPB2 sequence evidence supported identification as Exserohilum rostratum.

The report is geographically and temporally bounded to sampled North Carolina production in 2017–2018 and does not establish a universal leaf-age order, canopy-position sequence, cultivar response, incidence threshold, or severity scale.

title: First Report of Fusarium falciforme (FSSC 3 + 4) Causing Rot of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in California
supportedClaims: Fusarium falciforme isolates caused internal hemp stem rot in pathogenicity work and were reisolated from inoculated stems.
Field root rot was associated with the same organism, but the report specifically confirmed stem-rot ability more directly than root-rot ability.

title: First Report of Downy Mildew Caused by Pseudoperonospora cannabina on Cannabis sativa in New York
supportedClaims: In an August 2020 Ithaca, New York field trial, downy-mildew-like symptoms affected leaves and inflorescences of multiple hemp cultivars, including Auto CBD.
ITS and cox2 sequences were 100% identical to Pseudoperonospora cannabina references and ypt1 was 97.95% identical; the representative isolate was deposited as CUP-070922.

Whole-plant pathogenicity testing used ten four-week-old Anka plants and water controls; sporangia and the previously described symptoms occurred seven days after inoculation, controls remained asymptomatic, and the reisolate was confirmed by morphology plus ITS, cox2, and ypt1 sequencing.

The New York report establishes Pseudoperonospora cannabina as a causal oomycete on Cannabis, but field symptoms or dark underside material alone are not equivalent to its morpho-molecular confirmation.

title: First Report of Pythium aphanidermatum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Industrial hemp with Pythium aphanidermatum crown/root rot showed chlorosis, stunting, wilt, brown root lesions, feeder-root loss, and sometimes brown water-soaked stem lesions.
The above-ground syndrome overlaps other root diseases and water stress, reinforcing the need for cleaned-root and laboratory evidence.

title: Evaluation of downy mildew resistance in the USDA Hemp Germplasm Repository using high-throughput and traditional phenotyping methods
supportedClaims: Pseudoperonospora cannabina causes angular brown foliar lesions and dark sporulation on leaf undersides and can be associated with leaf curling, defoliation, and yield loss.
The study evaluated 108 hemp entries by robotic convolutional-neural-network leaf-disc analysis, visual scoring of the same discs, and detached-leaf assays; susceptibility ranged from 0 to 100%.

G 33532 and Santhica 27 had 0% severity across all three methods, while detached-leaf, CNN, and visual methods produced systematically different severity estimates; cultivar and assay context must therefore remain attached to image labels.
The CNN method consistently underestimated severity relative to visual assessment, so experimental machine scores are not a universal field or production-image threshold.

title: First Report of Anthracnose Leaf Spot Caused by Colletotrichum fioriniae on Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: Hemp anthracnose lesions began as light-green specks and developed into 3 to 4 mm round or angular spots with tan centers, darker brown margins, and yellow halos; centers could crack or drop out and lesions could coalesce.
Colletotrichum fioriniae was identified by morphology and four gene sequences, and inoculation reproduced characteristic leaf spots while controls remained symptomless.
Shot-hole or frog-eye appearance is not species-specific and must be differentiated from other fungal and bacterial leaf spots.

title: First Report of Fusarium commune Causing Damping Off and Wilt in Cannabis sativa in Pennsylvania
supportedClaims: Fusarium commune was reported from indoor Cannabis with wilted yellowing foliage, browning stems and roots, and withering, expanding the documented Fusarium species associated with Cannabis wilt/root disease.
The case supports maintaining a Fusarium complex label unless laboratory work resolves the causal species.

title: First Report of Fusarium graminearum Causing Head Blight on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Wisconsin
supportedClaims: Fusarium graminearum was reported causing blight of hemp grain heads, strengthening evidence that Fusarium flower/head disease is a distinct Cannabis diagnostic target from Fusarium root/crown rot.
The disease note used isolation and pathogen identification from symptomatic grain heads rather than relying on flower appearance alone.

title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

title: First Report of Pythium ultimum Crown and Root Rot of Industrial Hemp in the United States
supportedClaims: Pythium ultimum was pathogenic to industrial hemp in replicated inoculation work; symptoms began within about one week and the organism was reisolated and PCR-confirmed.
Cool early planting, low-lying/flood-prone conditions, and soil crusting after intense rainfall were risk context in the report, not species-level visual identifiers.

title: Reemergence of Septoria Leaf Spot Caused by Septoria cannabis on Hemp in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Septoria leaf spot was documented on hemp primarily on lower leaves and inner canopy, with small irregular brown-to-gray lesions expanding to roughly 5 to 7.5 mm and dark pycnidia in lesions.
Eight isolates were tested for pathogenicity on greenhouse-grown hemp and diagnostic loci were sequenced; morphology and sequence evidence supported Septoria cannabis in the Kentucky material.
Visual lesion appearance alone cannot separate Septoria from other hemp leaf-spot pathogens.

title: First Report of Southern Blight Caused by Sclerotium rolfsii on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Sicily and Southern Italy
supportedClaims: Infected hemp developed dark brown-to-tan discoloration at the soil line, crown and taproot rot, foliar yellowing, whole-plant collapse, white cottony mycelium, and tan-to-dark-brown spherical sclerotia.
Pathogenicity was reproduced on hemp and Sclerotium rolfsii was reisolated while noninoculated controls remained symptomless.
High summer temperatures and high soil moisture were associated with the reported outbreak but are risk context, not diagnostic proof.

title: First Report of Hemp Leaf Spot Caused by a Bipolaris Species on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Outdoor hemp in Kentucky developed severe necrotic leaf spot and blight associated with a lineage identified morphologically as Drechslera gigantea and placed within Bipolaris by ITS and partial 28S sequence analysis.
Inoculated hemp leaves developed symptoms while noninoculated controls remained symptomless, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.
The fungus was also associated with symptomatic dicot and monocot weeds in affected fields, but co-occurrence does not establish the direction or source of transmission.

This regional first report supports a Cannabis-specific Bipolaris disease; it does not establish universal lesion morphology, canopy preference, timing, prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, yield loss, or action thresholds.

title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.
North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

A 2017–2018 North Carolina survey based on 572 agronomic and 117 plant-clinic hemp submissions attributed common environmental disorders to excessive rainfall flooding roots and to poor root development in transplanted clones.
The same diagnostic survey found Pythium diseases in greenhouse hemp, supporting explicit separation of abiotic flooding injury from root-pathogen diagnoses.

title: Hemp Abnormal Growth Is Attributed to Mono-, Di-, or Tri-Infections of Spiroplasma citri, Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii, and Beet Curly Top Virus
supportedClaims: Across 67 symptomatic Nevada hemp samples, abnormal growth included stunting, yellowing, excessive apical branching, witches’ broom clusters, upward leaf rolling, mottling, and mosaic.
Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii was detected in 14 samples, Beet curly top virus in 57, and Spiroplasma citri in two; dual and triple infections occurred.

The overlapping syndrome cannot assign one causal agent visually, so diagnostic testing should consider phytoplasma, Spiroplasma citri, and Beet curly top virus rather than treating witches’ broom as a species-specific image label.

title: Characterization of Powdery Mildew Fungi Affecting Hemp in the Pacific Northwest
supportedClaims: Surveys of 74 hemp fields in Oregon and Washington across three time points in 2021 and 2022 found powdery mildew later in the season in Oregon but not at the early survey point.
Diagnostic PCR detected both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis on hemp, so a white powdery-mildew phenotype does not resolve the causal species.
Among assayed survey samples, G. ambrosiae was much more frequent than P. macularis, but the regional and seasonal sample does not establish a universal species prior for other production systems.

title: Development and validation of genetic markers for sex and cannabinoid chemotype in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Male and female Cannabis plants are phenotypically difficult to distinguish before flowering, while DNA from young plants can be used for genotype assays.
The validated CSP-1 Y-chromosome assay separated male plants from female and monoecious plants across 2,170 plants, but it did not separate female from monoecious expression.

Sex-linked genotype and expressed floral phenotype are not interchangeable because female-genotype plants can express monoecious flowers and hormonal manipulation can induce male flowers on XX plants.

title: Emerging Fungal and Oomycete Diseases of Cannabis in South Africa: First Reports and Pathogenicity Confirmation
supportedClaims: Cannabis samples from an aeroponic facility with wilting, yellowing, white mold, and gray mold were investigated with DNA sequence data and pathogenicity testing.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Pythium myriotylum were all confirmed capable of causing disease, demonstrating strong visual overlap among mold and wilt syndromes.
Sclerotinia diagnosis therefore requires organism-level evidence rather than white mold appearance alone.

title: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Experimental silencing of Cannabis phytoene desaturase and magnesium-chelatase-subunit-I genes produced spotted leaf bleaching, 70–73% lower target-transcript expression, and corresponding carotenoid or chlorophyll-a reductions.

This deliberately induced, virus-vector phenotype shows that perturbing pigment-related gene expression can create visible bleaching; it does not establish that naturally occurring sectors are genetic or safe from infectious differentials.

title: The power of zinc: excess and deficiency of Zn decrease cannabinoids in cannabis without Zn toxicity concerns to consumers
organization: Journal of Cannabis Research (Shiponi and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: Six clonal Annapurna plants per treatment were grown in perlite at five Zn-EDTA concentrations (0.05, 0.1, 0.35, 1, and 4 mg/L); treatments ran for 71 days, including 57 days under a flowering photoperiod, with fertigation adjusted to pH 6.0 and treatment concentrations analytically checked.

At 0.05 mg/L zinc, young leaves showed mottled interveinal chlorosis, plants were shorter, elongation rate was repressed by day 29, stems were thinner, and total biomass was lower; inflorescence yield was reduced in the 0.05-0.1 mg/L range while main-stem node count was unchanged.
Leaves contained 14.7 and 23.5 mg/kg dry-weight zinc at 0.05 and 0.1 mg/L supply, respectively, and yield was reduced at both concentrations, but visible chlorosis was reported only at 0.05 mg/L.

The authors found leaf phosphorus reached 15.6 mg/g at 0.05 mg/L zinc and explicitly cautioned that the visible leaf symptoms may represent phosphorus toxicity rather than a direct zinc-deficiency symptom; the image label is therefore mechanistically uncertain.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 maturity-stage composite comparing whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, roots, and apical inflorescences across all five zinc-supply treatments; it also contains high-zinc tip necrosis and must not receive a single whole-image deficiency label.

title: Impact of varying water stress periods (water shortage vs. waterlogging) on Cannabis sativa growth, leaf physiology, and CBD content
publisher: University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca
supportedClaims: In a controlled Cannabis sativa cv. G1 experiment, waterlogging was imposed by standing potted plants in a two-centimetre sheet of water; diagnosis therefore depended on verified root-zone exposure rather than canopy appearance alone.

After seven vegetative-stage days, waterlogged plants had shorter roots, lower leaf area, lower leaf-area index, lower chlorophyll-meter readings, and less biomass than controls; their growth remained lowest after a seven-day recovery period.

During reproductive-stage exposure, waterlogging reduced leaf-area index, root and shoot biomass, stomatal conductance, relative chlorophyll content, and photosystem-II efficiency as duration increased, but responses varied with stage and duration.

Water shortage produced overlapping reductions in several above-ground measurements, so reduced canopy growth or greenness cannot distinguish excess water from insufficient water without root-zone measurements.

title: Salinity effects on yield and nutrient uptake in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Early Haze Cannabis was grown hydroponically in rockwool at 1.8, 3, 6, 9, or 12 mS/cm, with EC raised either by increasing N, P, K, Ca, Mg, and S together or by adding NaCl to the 1.8 mS/cm nutrient solution.
Shoot and bud weight declined under both EC-raising pathways, but the response boundaries differed, demonstrating that equal EC does not identify the salt composition or a single causal ion.

Visible leaf necrosis occurred only in the 9 and 12 mS/cm NaCl treatments; absence of necrosis did not exclude yield effects, and necrosis at those extreme study treatments is not a universal field threshold.

Low leaf phosphorus in some low-EC treatments was associated with root-zone pH above 7.5, showing why pH and tissue chemistry must be checked rather than treating EC or leaf appearance as a single-nutrient diagnosis.

The trial used one cultivar, rockwool, hydroponic nutrient solutions, and deliberately constructed EC treatments; transfer to other cultivars, media, salt mixtures, and irrigation systems requires human review.

title: Increasing Inflorescence Dry Weight and Cannabinoid Content in Medical Cannabis Using Controlled Drought Stress
supportedClaims: In one controlled container-grown drug-type Cannabis experiment, fertigation was withheld during flowering week 7 until midday plant water potential reached approximately -1.5 MPa after 11 days; substrate volumetric moisture, plant water potential, photosynthesis, and leaf angle were measured against irrigated controls.

At the treatment endpoint, plants were visibly wilted and the measured indicator-leaf angle was approximately 52% greater than its initial angle; veinal chlorosis had appeared after about nine days, first on older leaves and to a lesser extent on newly formed leaves across the plant.

The day after re-fertigation, mean midday plant water potential recovered to the control level while net photosynthesis had only partially recovered, showing that response variables and recovery timing need not move together.

The timing, -1.5 MPa endpoint, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, and cannabinoid results come from one chemovar and one controlled flowering protocol; none is a universal Cannabis drought threshold, visual signature, or production recommendation.
The article figures are publisher-hosted copyrighted scientific content without a verified item-level reusable asset license, so they are citation evidence only and are not indexed as dataset media.

title: First Report of Meloidogyne incognita Infecting Cannabis sativa in Alabama
supportedClaims: Field-grown Alabama hemp in symptomatic areas showed stunted growth, poor root development, and numerous root galls, with Meloidogyne recovered from associated soil.
The nematode was identified as M. incognita using morphology and species-specific PCR; a greenhouse host-differential assay supported Race 3.
A modified Koch-postulates test reproduced galling and nematode reproduction on hemp, providing plant-linked pathogenicity evidence rather than a symptom-only association.

title: Review of Nematode Interactions with Hemp (Cannabis sativa)
supportedClaims: The review found that Meloidogyne is the most frequently reported plant-parasitic nematode genus on hemp, while stressing that only a small primary literature supports hemp-specific host and damage conclusions.

Galls induced on hemp by M. hapla, M. incognita, and M. javanica are described as small, whitish, and hard, generally not exceeding about 4 mm in diameter; M. enterolobii can form both small and large galls.
Its Figure 2 shows a controlled M. incognita inoculation on Cannabis sativa cultivar Cherry as an entire root system and close-up of small white galls with a 5 mm scale.

Hemp susceptibility and nematode reproduction vary substantially with cultivar, Meloidogyne species or isolate, inoculum, pot size, and evaluation time, so gall burden or canopy severity must not be generalized across cultivars or studies.

title: Plant Tissue Analysis and Interpretation for Vegetable Crops in Florida
publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: For vegetable crops, nutrient symptoms can be masked by other nutritional disorders, unfavorable environments, or pests, so tissue analysis is used to complement rather than replace contextual diagnosis.

The publication describes cross-crop molybdenum deficiency as chlorosis and rolling or necrosis of intermediate-age and older leaves and associates it with acidic conditions, but those descriptions are not Cannabis validation and must not be transferred into Cannabis image ground truth.

The publication recommends matched disorder and normal samples of the same cultivar and physiological age, with corresponding soil or root-zone context, and notes that foliar nutrient residues can make tissue results misleading.
Its vegetable critical-value tables do not establish a Cannabis molybdenum threshold; crop, tissue, stage, and analytical method must be interpreted specifically.

title: Pathogenicity and Mefenoxam Sensitivity of Pythium, Globisporangium, and Fusarium Isolates From Coconut Coir and Rockwool in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Production
supportedClaims: Controlled pathogenicity experiments on hemp cultivar 'Wife' confirmed that selected Pythium myriotylum and Globisporangium irregulare isolates from production substrates could reduce growth and cause chlorosis or wilt; inoculated organisms were recovered from root fragments.

The source facility sampling involved coconut coir and rockwool rather than original diseased marijuana plant tissue, and Koch-style pathogenicity testing used one hemp cultivar, so the host, facility, timing, and severity cannot be generalized.

Figure 7 is a whole-plant, multi-treatment composite at 14 days after inoculation that includes Pythium, Globisporangium, Fusarium, and an uninoculated control; it does not show roots or crown tissue and cannot confirm an unknown plant from appearance.

title: Discovery and Genetic Mapping of PM1, a Powdery Mildew Resistance Gene in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Patchy white mycelial colonies developed on Cannabis foliage and flowers and were associated with reduced vigor, but colony presence did not by itself identify every possible powdery-mildew species.

In two segregating Cannabis populations, susceptible plants developed white colonies on leaves and stems within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure, while PM1-bearing plants showed complete resistance to the tested Pacific Northwest G. ambrosiae isolate.

Plants were followed through flowering, and 55 clonal replicates were reinfected to validate scores; resistance or absence of visible colonies in this experiment is genotype- and isolate-specific rather than a universal negative control.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Cannabis comparison; its panels share experimental source context and must not be treated as independent training samples without source grouping and review.

title: Diseases of Cannabis sativa Caused by Diverse Fusarium Species
supportedClaims: Multiple Fusarium species are associated with Cannabis root, crown, stem, wilt, and flower disease syndromes.
Reported Cannabis Fusarium diagnoses use culture and sequence-based or other laboratory identification together with pathogenicity evidence; symptom appearance is not species-level confirmation.

title: Comparative genomics of a cannabis pathogen reveals insight into the evolution of pathogenicity in Xanthomonas
supportedClaims: Cannabis bacterial leaf spot was described as water-soaked lesions followed by necrosis with a yellow halo.
The study sequenced two geographically distinct strains previously isolated from symptomatic cannabis tissue in Japan and Romania and proposed the species name Xanthomonas cannabis.

title: Pathogens and Molds Affecting Production and Quality of Cannabis sativa L.
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across sampled indoor, greenhouse, and field Cannabis crops, flower buds with brown discoloration, blighted bracts and leaves, tissue decay, and grayish-brown mycelium yielded cultures identified as Botrytis cinerea by morphology and ITS-rDNA sequencing.

The study documented a visual sequence from browning and decay of leaves and bracts in developing inflorescences to destruction of the entire inflorescence, as well as internal mycelium and decay in harvested flowers.

Under severe late-harvest disease pressure, Cannabis leaves developed small circular spots that enlarged and coalesced into necrotic, often vein-delimited areas, sometimes with yellow margins; this leaf presentation was contextual rather than a standalone diagnostic rule.

Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Penicillium olsonii recovered from harvested buds each produced browning and decay after inoculation under high humidity, demonstrating that brown bud rot is not species-specific in an image.

Figure 4 is a multi-panel Cannabis reference containing early and advanced inflorescence disease, internal harvested-bud decay, culture and microscopy views, and leaf lesions; the article and figure are licensed CC BY 4.0.

title: Hermaphroditism in Marijuana (Cannabis sativa L.) Inflorescences – Impact on Floral Morphology, Seed Formation, Progeny Sex Ratios, and Genetic Variation
supportedClaims: Young pistillate inflorescences developed protruding white hair-like stigmas that later became yellowish-white, then curled and browned or reddened as carpels and surrounding bracts swelled during maturation.
Staminate flowers formed in pedicillate clusters at leaf axils, opened five tepals, exposed five stamens, and released pollen through a longitudinal anther groove.

In predominantly female inflorescences, co-sexual expression appeared as bright-yellow 2–3 mm anthers within bract tissue among stigmas; expression ranged from a few anthers to replacement of much of the female inflorescence and progressed over weeks.
The study figures are original Cannabis photographs and microscopy distributed with the article under the Creative Commons Attribution license.

title: Aquaponic and Hydroponic Solutions Modulate NaCl-Induced Stress in Drug-Type Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: A controlled indoor flowering experiment tested one type-II chemovar at 1 to 40 mM NaCl in hydroponic and aquaponic solutions and measured canopy growth, chlorophyll content index, gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, water-use physiology, solution pH/EC, yield, and cannabinoids.
At 40 mM NaCl, hydroponic plants had reduced growth index and chlorophyll content index over time, while the same measured responses were not significantly affected by NaCl in the aquaponic solution.
The solution-dependent result and single-chemovar flowering design show that production system, genotype, stage, and treatment composition must accompany any image or video label.
The study did not establish a universal visible symptom signature; image appearance alone cannot identify NaCl exposure or elevated root-zone EC as the primary cause.

title: Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) to Nitrogen Supply Under Long Photoperiod
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Saloner and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: A controlled long-photoperiod experiment compared one medical Cannabis cultivar at 30, 80, 160, 240, and 320 mg/L total nitrogen in soilless media, with five replicate plants per treatment and repeated plant-development measurements.

At 320 mg/L nitrogen the plants and plant organs were smaller and dark green; at 240 mg/L shoot coloration and development appeared similar to the 160 mg/L treatment while root development was already restricted.

Supply above 160 mg/L restricted growth and biomass in this experiment, while nitrogen use efficiency declined and leaf, stem, and root total nitrogen and nitrate generally increased across the tested range.
The 160–320 mg/L treatments had similar dark-green leaf color, so dark foliage by itself did not distinguish the study optimum from excessive supply.

At high nitrogen, photosynthetic pigments continued to increase but photosynthesis did not; the authors associated the high-supply decline with stomatal closure and reduced stomatal conductance, transpiration, and intercellular carbon dioxide.

Irrigation EC rose with nitrogen treatment from 2080 µS/cm at 160 mg/L to 2510 and 2760 µS/cm at 240 and 320 mg/L, and high-treatment leachate nitrogen exceeded input concentration; nitrogen-dose effects therefore cannot be separated from the experiment-specific salt and formulation context by an image alone.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing whole plants, youngest fully developed leaves, and roots across the five nitrogen doses; the columns are treatment levels rather than independent diagnosis classes.

title: Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Rodriguez-Morrison et al.)
supportedClaims: Indoor-grown Cannabis sativa Stillwater was exposed during flowering to average canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.
Dry inflorescence yield increased linearly through the highest tested PPFD even though leaf-level photosynthesis saturated below 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.

The high-light experiment did not establish a universal PPFD injury threshold or validate cupping, bleaching, or edge necrosis as light-specific visual symptoms; light exposure must be interpreted with cultivar, acclimation, canopy position, temperature, carbon dioxide, and water status.

In Stillwater during the 12-hour flowering phase, chlorophyll-content index was higher in week 1 than weeks 5 and 9 and was consistently higher in upper- than lower-canopy fan leaves; the authors described evidence of early senescence but stated that the contributions of leaf age and plant ontogeny to diminished week-9 photosynthesis were unresolved.
The study measured chlorophyll index and physiology rather than validating a yellow-leaf appearance, harvest date, or universal late-flower-fade sequence.

title: Optimisation of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium for Soilless Production of Cannabis sativa in the Flowering Stage Using Response Surface Analysis
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Bevan et al.)
supportedClaims: A high-THC Cannabis cultivar grown in deep-water culture during flowering showed quadratic inflorescence-yield responses to nitrogen and phosphorus, with predicted optima near 194 mg per litre nitrogen and 59 mg per litre phosphorus under the tested conditions.

Inflorescence yield decreased markedly outside approximately 160–230 mg per litre nitrogen and 40–80 mg per litre phosphorus, demonstrating that flowering plants still respond materially to nutrient supply.
Those solution concentrations are experiment- and cultivar-specific and must not be converted into universal feed targets, tissue sufficiency ranges, or visual thresholds.

title: Nitrogen Source Matters: High NH4/NO3 Ratio Reduces Cannabinoids, Terpenoids, and Yield in Medical Cannabis
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Saloner and Bernstein)
supportedClaims: A controlled reproductive-stage experiment held total nitrogen at 200 mg/L and compared 0, 10, 30, 50, and 100% ammonium fractions, with five replicate medical Cannabis plants per treatment.

Plants receiving 0–30% ammonium appeared similar and did not show toxicity symptoms, while 50% ammonium plants appeared normal through most of the experiment before leaf necrosis and wilting emerged during the last two weeks.

At 50% ammonium, 40% of plants wilted in the final week and inflorescence biomass was 46% lower than in the nitrate-only treatment; this late response cannot be inferred reliably from an earlier normal-looking image.
The 100% ammonium treatment caused early stunting, curly leaves with marginal necrosis at growing tips, severe root damage, spread of necrosis to all plant parts, wilting, and plant death.

The early 100% ammonium growing-tip image was taken 17 days after treatment began, while whole-plant, inflorescence, and root images were captured at maturation and the sampled leaf image ten days earlier.
The authors cautioned that damage under 50–100% ammonium may also reflect reduced or absent nitrate supply, making ammonium-form toxicity mechanistically different from excessive total nitrogen dose.
Figures 1 and 2 are CC BY 4.0 visual references; Figure 1 mixes five ammonium ratios, organs, and capture times, while Figure 2 shows one apical view from the 100% ammonium treatment.

title: Assessing the adaptive role of cannabidiol (CBD) in Cannabis sativa defense against cannabis aphids
supportedClaims: Phorodon cannabis is a Cannabis-adapted aphid and was studied directly on Cannabis sativa hemp in whole-plant assays.
The study supports cannabis aphid as a biologically relevant hemp pest but does not make generic leaf yellowing or curling species-level ground truth.

title: Effect of saline irrigation and plant-based biostimulant application on fiber hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) growth and phytocannabinoid composition
supportedClaims: Felina 32 fiber hemp in an outdoor mesocosm was irrigated with NaCl solutions at 2, 4, and 6 dS/m and compared with a 0.4 dS/m tap-water control.
The 2, 4, and 6 dS/m irrigation treatments limited crop growth by 7%, 30%, and 48%, respectively; biomass effects followed measured salinity rather than a diagnostic leaf-color class.

The experiment documented altered sodium, chloride, phosphate, nitrate, potassium, and calcium assimilation in leaves, supporting broad mineral imbalance as a measured consequence rather than proof of a single-element deficiency.

Because the study used one fiber cultivar, NaCl-defined irrigation treatments, an outdoor mesocosm, and a biostimulant factor, its EC values are treatment conditions rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

title: Mapping and Characterization of a Novel Powdery Mildew Resistance Locus (PM2) in Cannabis sativa L.
organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Seifi et al.)
supportedClaims: The study used a leaf-area severity scale of 0 for no symptoms, 1 for less than 25% coverage with few restricted nonspreading colonies, 2 for 25–50%, 3 for 50–75%, and 4 for 75–100% powdery-mildew coverage.

Under severe adult-plant disease pressure, susceptible genotypes could show colonization of flower sugar leaves, petioles, and stem tissue; adult susceptibility sometimes exceeded the earlier clone-assay result.

PM2 resistance strongly suppressed conidia generation and involved a localized microscopic hypersensitive response without macroscopic chlorotic spots, so symptom-negative or visually clean tissue is not proof that all pathogen interaction is absent.
The scale and response were generated in controlled inoculation and resistance-mapping experiments and are not universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention thresholds.

title: Cultivar Identity and Spider Mite Herbivory Shape Rhizosphere Bacteria in Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
supportedClaims: A trained evaluator scored naturally occurring Tetranychus urticae injury on flowering BaOx and Cherry Citrus hemp under the same greenhouse conditions with a standardized 0-to-5 scale: 0, no visible stippling, chlorosis, or webbing; 1, slight stippling on a few leaves; 2, moderate stippling across multiple leaves; 3, heavy stippling with early chlorosis; 4, extensive chlorosis with patchy webbing; and 5, severe chlorosis and necrosis with dense silk webbing.

Cherry Citrus had significantly less visual damage than BaOx despite similar measured growth traits, showing that cultivar identity can alter symptom severity and limiting generalization of a single image progression.

The study used background mite populations rather than experimentally manipulating herbivore pressure and reported associations rather than proof of causality; its two-cultivar flowering-stage score is a study-specific reference, not a universal diagnostic or intervention threshold.

Figure 1 is a CC BY 4.0 composite reference for the 0-to-5 visual damage scale and should not be split into independent training examples without panel-level cropping, source grouping, and label review.

title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

In Cannabis sativa T1, manganese-toxicity symptoms appeared seven weeks after treatment: marginal yellowing began on lower leaves, intensified inward toward the midrib, and advanced to marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional leaf abscission.

The manganese-toxicity treatment used a tenfold increase over the complete formula (180 micromolar Mn versus 18 micromolar), but treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range; dry weight did not differ significantly from controls and the authors called for higher-concentration work to refine the threshold.
Figure 5 is a six-panel composite: manganese toxicity occupies the left column and boron toxicity the right, with initial, intermediate, and advanced symptom rows.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

title: Variation in Hydric Response of Two Industrial Hemp Varieties (Cannabis sativa) to Induced Water Stress
supportedClaims: Two hemp varieties showed notably different water-stress strategies, including partial stomatal closure in one and rapid leaf shedding in another.
The genotype-dependent responses support using substrate moisture and plant water-status context rather than a single visual symptom to identify water deficit.

title: First Molecular Phylogenetic Identification and Report of Pseudocercospora cannabina Causing Leaf Spot Disease on Cannabis sativa in Thailand
supportedClaims: Twenty symptomatic Cannabis leaves were collected from one plantation in Chiang Rai, Thailand, in February 2022; field symptoms were circular-to-elliptical olive leaf spots with gray centers and dark brown-to-black margins, and severely affected plants defoliated.

Upper-surface lesions were initially inconspicuous to slightly discolored and vein-limited, later becoming pale yellowish, irregular to subcircular, approximately 2 to 6 mm, without a distinct margin, and capable of covering the leaf.
Lower-surface lesions were indistinct to pale yellowish and bore hypophyllous, vein-limited, grayish-to-pale-brown, velvety or sooty conidial patches.

In the pathogenicity experiment, hyphae entered through lower-surface stomata within 24 hours, inoculated leaves developed leaf spots at 5 days, water controls remained symptomless, and the reisolate matched the inoculum by morphology and ITS sequence.
