Two isolates were identified as Pseudocercospora cannabina using morphology plus ITS, act, tef1, and rpb2 sequence evidence; the authors note missing type-material sequence data and a weakly supported broader phylogenetic clade, limiting visual or single-locus species claims.

Figure 1 is a mixed natural-symptom, whole-canopy, upper/underside, culture, cross-section, conidiophore, and conidium composite; Figure 2 combines controlled lower-surface penetration microscopy with symptom reproduction at 5 days post-inoculation.
The article and its figures are distributed under CC BY 4.0; whole composites still require panel-level review before automated training.

title: Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics
organization: International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: The authors documented Cannabis leaves with mosaic, mottling, and line patterns that superficially resembled viral symptoms, and separately illustrated sharply chlorotic, chlorophyll-deficient sectors attributed to somatic mutation in Figure 4e.

Defined broad-spectrum and specific RT-PCR assays did not detect the targeted viruses in tested OG Kush and Headband tissues; positive controls worked, no virus-like particles were seen in the examined Cannabis samples by transmission electron microscopy, and inoculated indicator hosts remained symptomless for three weeks.

Those negative results apply only to the sampled tissues, agents, assays, and observation period and therefore do not establish genetic causality or exclude every virus, viroid, pest, nutrient, root-zone, or chemical cause.

title: Ecology of Fungus Gnats (Bradysia spp.) in Greenhouse Production Systems Associated with Disease-Interactions and Alternative Management Strategies
supportedClaims: Bradysia fungus gnats are important greenhouse horticultural pests whose larvae feed on roots and may contribute to disease interactions.

The review describes adults as weak, delicate fliers associated with moist growing media and larvae as translucent to white, legless, dark-headed organisms in the medium; these organism traits are more useful than nonspecific canopy decline.

Larval feeding can damage roots and young plant material, while fungus gnats can participate in pathogen interactions; finding one component does not establish that it caused every observed root or canopy symptom.

This is cross-crop greenhouse evidence rather than Cannabis-specific symptom validation, so plant yellowing or stunting cannot identify fungus gnats without observing adults, larvae, or other root-zone evidence.

title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

title: Virulence of Five Root-Knot Nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) on Nine Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) Varieties and Nematicidal Potential of Hemp Seed Extracts Against Meloidogyne javanica
supportedClaims: A controlled greenhouse experiment found M. javanica, M. incognita, M. arenaria, M. hapla, and M. luci pathogenic across nine tested industrial-hemp varieties, with all inoculated treatments showing reduced shoot weight relative to controls.

M. incognita produced the lowest mean root weight among the tested species, while M. javanica and M. luci produced the lowest mean shoot weights, demonstrating that root and canopy effects differ by species.

Females per gram of root, egg masses per gram of root, and fecundity differed by both hemp variety and Meloidogyne species; Futura 75 carried the lowest overall nematode numbers, whereas USO 31, Fedora 17, Ferimon 12, and Zenit were among the more susceptible varieties in this experiment.
The article figures concern laboratory seed-extract effects on juvenile mobility and egg hatch rather than visual diagnosis of infected Cannabis roots, so those graphs are not symptom ground truth.

title: Transmission, Spread, Longevity and Management of Hop Latent Viroid, a Widespread and Destructive Pathogen Affecting Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plants in North America
supportedClaims: RT-PCR/RT-qPCR detected HLVd in asymptomatic stock plants and rooted vegetative cuttings; in the stock genotypes tested, roots were the most consistent positive tissue while individual upper or lower leaf samples were not consistently positive.

After stem inoculation with infectious sap, HLVd was detected in roots within 2–3 weeks and foliage within 4–6 weeks, and spread was faster under a flowering-inducing 12:12 photoperiod than under 24-hour lighting in that experiment.

The study detected HLVd in inflorescence tissue, glandular trichomes, dried flowers, pollen, seeds, and other production-system materials, supporting plant-part and propagation context but not image-only confirmation.

Figure 1 combines stock and flowering plant appearance with tissue-specific RT-PCR results and sequence-confirmed bands; it is a molecularly anchored CC BY 4.0 reference but not a single-class visual training sample.

Chemical treatments in the study were evaluated partly by loss of amplifiable HLVd RNA; absence of an RT-PCR band after treatment must not be generalized into a universal facility sanitation guarantee without a validated protocol.

title: Genotypic Variation in Photosynthesis and Biomass Partitioning Underlies Agronomic Performance and Cannabinoid Profile in Cannabis sativa Under Drought
supportedClaims: Water deficit imposed at early flowering reduced leaf area and affected plant water status, photosynthesis, biomass partitioning, and cannabinoid response in a genotype-dependent way.
Different Cannabis genotypes used different physiological drought responses, so visual canopy appearance or one moisture reading is not a universal drought-severity scale.

title: Leaf Age and Position Effects on Quantum Yield and Photosynthetic Capacity in Hemp Crowns
supportedClaims: Hemp leaves at three crown positions were followed from full expansion for 42 days; photosynthetic capacity declined with leaf age regardless of crown position, light intensity, or photoperiod.
The measured leaves remained green while photosynthetic capacity declined, demonstrating that physiological aging is not equivalent to visible yellowing.

The experiment evaluated aging leaves before abscission in hemp crowns and did not establish a drug-type Cannabis harvest cue, a cultivar-independent color sequence, or proof that visible chlorosis is normal.

title: Hop Latent Viroid: A Hidden Threat to the Cannabis Industry
supportedClaims: Published Cannabis reports associate HLVd with dudding symptoms that can include stunting, shortened internodes, brittle stems, smaller or malformed leaves, weak rooting, and reduced inflorescence quality, while some infected plants remain asymptomatic.
Because symptom expression can vary with genotype, growth stage, environment, and viroid concentration, molecular testing rather than visual appearance is required to establish an HLVd label.
This article is a review and must not be used as a substitute for the plant-linked molecular evidence or study-specific limits in the primary sources attached to this profile.

title: Septoria cannabicola, a new species on Cannabis sativa from Japan
supportedClaims: Molecular phylogeny and morphology demonstrated that Cannabis leaf spot historically attributed to Septoria cannabis can involve a distinct species, Septoria cannabicola.
Natural symptoms began as indistinct yellow spots on lower leaves and progressed to brown irregular lesions and premature defoliation of older leaves.
Species-level Septoria naming therefore requires laboratory evidence rather than lesion appearance alone.

title: Onion thrips, Thrips tabaci (Thysanoptera: Thripidae), reduces yields in indoor-grown cannabis
supportedClaims: A controlled preliminary study identified onion thrips, Thrips tabaci, proliferating on indoor-grown Cannabis and compared plants initially receiving zero, one, or five thrips.

Plants initially receiving five thrips had lower fresh yield than plants receiving zero thrips; the result supports monitoring but does not establish an image-only diagnosis or a general action threshold.
The experiment was limited to defined indoor conditions and infestation treatments, so yield effects and severity must not be generalized across cultivars, production systems, or thrips species.

title: Species: Xanthomonas cannabis
organization: List of Prokaryotic names with Standing in Nomenclature (LPSN)
supportedClaims: Xanthomonas cannabis (ex Severin 1978) McKnight et al. 2026 is the validly published correct species name.
The historical names Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis and the 2015 proposed name “Xanthomonas cannabis” are homotypic synonyms; type strain identifiers include ICMP 6570, LMG 9042, and NCPPB 2877.

title: Observations of Insect and Disease Pests on Field Grown Hemp in Kentucky
organization: Science of Hemp: Production and Pest Management Conference Proceedings
publisher: Auburn University College of Agriculture and Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
supportedClaims: A 2021 University of Kentucky survey at the Spindletop Farm and Robinson Center observed separate cases of anthracnose identified as Colletotrichum fioriniae in field-grown hemp research plantings.

The survey covered hemp grown for cannabinoid, grain, and fiber purposes and documented multiple fungal diseases in the same season, so field context does not make a photographed lesion specific to anthracnose.

The conference report explicitly described its results as preliminary and called for additional research; it does not establish prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, symptom timing, yield impact, or a visual decision threshold for anthracnose.

title: Most Prevalent Diseases
supportedClaims: Purdue describes upper-surface yellow-green spots that become angular and brown, with heavily lesioned leaves becoming distorted and plants defoliating.
Gray-to-black down-like growth on corresponding leaf undersides during wet periods is a crucial sign, while chemical damage and other leaf spots are important visual confounders.
High humidity and free water on leaves are conducive conditions; environmental context supports a differential but does not confirm the organism.
The institutional page lists images but retains Purdue copyright and does not state item-level reusable or automated-training terms, so no Purdue media were copied or admitted.

title: Cannabis aphid, Phorodon cannabis
supportedClaims: Cannabis aphids are small, soft-bodied, long-antennaed aphids with piercing-sucking mouthparts and occur on leaves and stems of hemp plants grown indoors and outdoors.

Cannabis aphids may be pale to light green or light brown; winged forms have dark spotting and wingless forms often show pale abdominal stripes, so body color alone is not a reliable species identifier.

title: Cabbage Looper, Trichoplusia ni (Hübner) (Insecta: Lepidoptera: Noctuidae)
publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: Institutional morphology guidance describes mature larvae as predominantly green, usually with a distinct white stripe on each side and faint dorsal white stripes, with a narrower anterior and broader posterior body that loops during movement.

Cabbage looper can be confused with soybean looper; dark thoracic legs and microscopic body microspines favor soybean looper, so a dorsal photograph or looping gait alone is insufficient for species confirmation.
Eggs are small, ridged, yellowish-white to green, and can occur on either leaf surface; eggs alone require rearing or expert identification because their appearance is not a Cannabis injury label.

A thin white fragile cocoon can occur under foliage or in debris, and the gray-brown adult has a central silvery U-shaped mark and dot that may be connected; an adult or cocoon not linked to a damaged Cannabis plant does not prove larval injury.
Geographic activity, generation time, host suitability, and crop management vary substantially; non-Cannabis timing, host, threshold, and treatment statements are transfer context only.

title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: On hemp, powdery fungal mycelium and spores can appear as whitish spots or patches on both leaf surfaces and can spread across leaves, petioles, stems, flower bracts, and buds within about a week under favorable conditions.
Increasing severity can lead to leaf necrosis and defoliation, while high humidity favors infection even though free leaf wetness is not required.

The guide recommends diagnostic-center confirmation for hemp diseases; its powdery-mildew image is credited to Nicole Gauthier and does not carry an explicit reusable-media license on the page, so it is not copied or indexed as training media here.

title: Carotenoid Pigments
supportedClaims: Carotenoid-pigment-inhibitor injury can produce white, pale-yellow, or pale-green new shoot tips and leaves, occasional pink-to-purple margins, reduced growth, and later necrosis; resumed green growth can appear above older bleached foliage in less-sensitive plants.

The guide identifies clomazone as a soil-absorbed Group 13 pigment inhibitor with high vapor-drift potential and recommends inspecting susceptible weeds and other plants along field edges for a shared exposure pattern.

Severe iron deficiency, bleaching infections, contact-herbicide injury, PPO-inhibitor bronzing, air pollution, and insect-growth-regulator exposure can overlap visually and require contextual exclusion.
The grape and pokeweed photographs are explicitly credited to J. Neal under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but they are non-Cannabis transfer references and do not establish clomazone injury in hemp.

title: Gray Mold of Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: Brown water-soaked lesions on hemp stems, leaves, or flowers can become necrotic and develop gray spores; stem lesions can girdle stems, cause breakage, and form black irregular sclerotia.
Seedlings and cuttings can damp off under cool, wet conditions, with necrotic or water-soaked roots, while moist and humid production conditions favor disease development.

Fusarium flower mold can resemble gray mold but lacks the characteristic gray spore masses, Fusarium cankers lack gray spores and sclerotia, and Sclerotinia produces white mycelial mats; these features guide triage but laboratory confirmation remains appropriate.

title: Hemp Russet Mite in Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: The absence of webbing helps distinguish hemp russet mite from spider mites, but microscopy is necessary because injury resembles disease and abiotic stress.
Stem, petiole, and leaf feeding can cause stunting, smaller leaves, dull gray or bronzed tissue, and suppressed or dwarfed buds.
The two referenced photographs are credited to Whitney Cranshaw, Colorado State University, Bugwood.org, under CC BY 4.0.

title: Bacterial Leaf Spot on Greenhouse Ornamentals
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse ornamental hosts, bacterial and fungal leaf spots can be visually confounded; bacterial streaming can support suspicion but may be absent, and diagnosis by a plant disease clinic is recommended.

As general bacterial-leaf-spot precautions rather than cannabis-specific epidemiology, splashing water and handling wet plants can spread bacteria, so suspect plants should be handled dry and separately.

title: Twospotted Spider Mite in Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: Twospotted spider mites occur on greenhouse and field hemp; at least 10x magnification is recommended because mites and eggs occur mainly on leaf undersides while feeding injury appears as pale speckling on the upper surface.

High infestations can produce yellow, dry leaves, premature leaf drop, reduced flower growth, and webbing that can cover much of a plant; hot, low-humidity conditions can shorten a generation to roughly one to two weeks.
Water-stressed or dusty plants and field edges near dusty paths can have greater risk, but exposure context is not proof of the causal organism.

No research-based action threshold was established for North Carolina hemp across fiber, seed, and cannabinoid production, so visible damage grades or mite counts must not be presented as universal treatment thresholds.

title: Dectes Stem Borer (Dectes texanus)
organization: Kansas State University Department of Entomology
publisher: Kansas State University Research and Extension
supportedClaims: In soybean, eggs are usually laid in mid-canopy leaf petioles; larvae tunnel down the petiole into the stem and generally move downward.
An individual wilted or drying leaf above the normal lower-canopy senescence zone is a useful scouting cue but is not diagnostic without stem tunneling and a larva.
Representative confirmation requires carefully splitting stems from several field locations and documenting tunnels and live larvae.

title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.

The Missouri Extension guide lists chlorotic spots, curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion as possible tarnished plant bug injury on hemp; these institutional symptom claims conflict with earlier hemp literature that had not documented foliar symptoms and therefore require organism-linked human review.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.

title: Hop Latent Viroid in Hemp
supportedClaims: Visual recognition is unreliable because infected hemp can remain asymptomatic or show subtle, variable symptoms influenced by viroid strain, plant genetics, environment, and viroid concentration.

The institutional hemp field and survey context includes yellow patterning or generalized yellowing, brittle branches, misshapen or smaller leaves, shorter internodes, stunting, and small buds, with foliar symptoms and stunting often more apparent from mid-season onward in the Pacific Northwest.

Cuttings from infected mother plants can root poorly while young plants may show no obvious above-ground symptoms; roots can test positive about two weeks after cuttings are made and may be more reliable than leaves for testing young plants.

The page recommends tested stock, separation and testing of propagation material, removal of confirmed infected plants, and cleaning tools, surfaces, and equipment that contact sap; it also states that no method reliably guarantees complete HLVd inactivation on contaminated tools.

The page credits the detached-leaf survey composite to Cynthia M. Ocamb and the two-stage field composite to K. Frost but states no explicit reusable-media license, so both assets are metadata-only license-review references.

title: Dectes Stem Borer Management in Soybeans (FS-1196)
supportedClaims: The peer-reviewed soybean factsheet describes gray adults with black-and-gray banded antennae and creamy white to yellow, legless, accordion-like larvae.
Petiole pith feeding can produce a single wilted leaf before larvae tunnel into the main stem; later internal girdling can predispose mature plants to basal breakage and lodging.
Regional occurrence and lodging losses are variable, so soybean severity, yield, and management values must not be transferred directly to Cannabis.

title: Pot-Bound Indoor Plants
organization: University of Maryland Extension, Home & Garden Information Center
authors: University of Maryland Extension Home & Garden Information Center
supportedClaims: The institutional guide describes pot-bound morphology in non-Cannabis indoor plants as roots encircling the pot perimeter and forming a tight mass that can fill the pot or extend over its edge.
It also reports that water can pass through a pot-bound root mass too quickly while the root-ball center remains dry, and that resulting desiccation can produce tip dieback or marginal browning.

These morphology and watering observations are transfer context only: they support root-ball inspection and drought exclusion but do not establish Cannabis ground truth, severity, progression, or a camera-only diagnosis.

title: Japanese beetles in yards and gardens
supportedClaims: Adult Japanese beetles are approximately one-third to one-half inch long, with a metallic-green head and thorax, copper-brown wing covers, five white hair patches along each abdominal side, and two patches at the abdominal tip.

In Minnesota, adults primarily feed during July and August and can persist into September; damaged leaves emit odors that attract other beetles, producing concentrated clusters while neighboring suitable plants may remain lightly infested.
The seasonal timing is regional context rather than a universal Cannabis calendar, and the larval white-grub stage requires separate ventral-spine examination for positive identification.

title: Fungus Gnats fact sheet
publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: Greenhouse fungus-gnat larvae can feed on roots or inside stems and may be associated with poor plant growth, yellowing, and stunting.
Adults around moist growing media are a useful inspection cue, but above-ground plant symptoms remain nonspecific.

title: Hemp Pests in New Hampshire
organization: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: Adult Japanese beetles feed on hemp leaves and developing flowers; leaf feeding produces skeletonization, and large populations may completely defoliate plants.
Japanese beetle grubs may damage roots, but turfgrass is their preferred larval habitat; an adult observed on hemp should not be used to infer that hemp roots contain grubs.
Representative field scouting should cover multiple plants and locations and record the pest, plant injury, crop context, and collected specimens rather than relying on one image.
UNH Extension associates Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale with indoor Cannabis sativa grown as a high-THC crop and reports observations from indoor cultivation across the United States.

The institutional guide reported no North American outdoor-hemp records and identified hemp soil-insect research as a gap; this supports an indoor-production scope flag rather than proof that outdoor infestation is impossible.

title: Broad Mite
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus) is documented on hemp and occupies shaded, protected leaf surfaces and crevices.
Adults are extremely small, oval to round, and light yellow to green; eggs are laid on leaf undersides.
Feeding can produce malformed, warped, or hardened young leaves and flower buds, bronzing, stunting, and aborted growth.

title: Curly Top Virus
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Infected field-grown hemp can become stunted and develop yellow mosaic or generalized leaf chlorosis.
Beet leafhoppers transmit curly-top viruses during probing and feeding; scouting is especially important while plants are small and should include leaf undersides, field edges, and nearby weeds.
Yellow mosaic hemp samples should be submitted to a plant diagnostic laboratory, and tomato spotted wilt virus is an early-season look-alike.

title: Hemp Russet Mite
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Hemp russet mites are microscopic, cigar-shaped eriophyid mites usually found on leaf undersides and best identified with high magnification.
High populations can cause fine spotting, bronzing, reduced leaf size, brittle foliage, upward edge curl, and stem bronzing.
Spider mites, thrips, and physiological leaf curl or yellowing are documented look-alikes.

title: Lygus Bug (Tarnished Plant Bug)
organization: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management
supportedClaims: Adult Lygus vary from brown with yellow, black, or red markings and a yellow or green triangle on the upper center of the back; nymphs are lighter, dark-spotted, wingless, and rounded.
The hemp guidance states that seed feeding can produce shriveling and heavy flower feeding may cause bud drop or flower abortion, while symptoms on foliage have not been documented.
Utah scouting guidance recommends visual or sweep-net sampling of hemp and nearby weeds plus repeated examination of flowers for adults and nymphs.
No economic damage had been documented in surveyed Utah hemp fields and no hemp treatment threshold had been developed; seed hemp warrants closer monitoring than cannabinoid hemp.
Institutional look-alikes include other plant or seed bugs, false chinch bugs, and beneficial big-eyed bugs.

title: Nutrient Deficiencies
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: USU describes hemp phosphorus-deficiency context as slowed growth with bluish-green foliage, purple petioles, copper to purplish-brown lower-leaf blotches, contortion or downward curl, and bronze or purple necrosis in heavily affected leaves.

USU states that high-pH soil above 7, cold soil, and clayey, poorly drained, soggy conditions can limit phosphorus uptake, so tissue appearance cannot distinguish inadequate supply from impaired root-zone availability.
The page recommends soil and nutrient analysis to guide amendments and states that excess phosphorus can resemble iron or zinc deficiency, supporting measurement before corrective fertilization.
The phosphorus photographs on the page have mixed USU and commercial-vendor credits and no explicit reuse license, so they are not admitted as verified media or ground truth.

USU describes hemp calcium-deficiency context as contorted or curled leaves, irregular yellow-brown spotting while intervening tissue remains green, slowed flower-bud development, and root-tip dieback, and states that excess water, salinity, or root damage can impair calcium transport.

The USU calcium page localizes pictured spotting to lower leaves, which is compatible with a flowering-stage hydroponic study but differs from the newly expanding growth sequence in the vegetative T1 study; canopy location alone is therefore not diagnostic.

title: Pythium Root and Crown Rot of Hemp
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: The institutional diagnostic note describes stunting and wilt with root rot, including loss of the root outer layer that leaves the central core, and separately describes crown infection that can girdle the stem.
The note states that either root rot or crown rot can progress to rapid wilt and death and cautions that the two syndromes need not occur together, supporting separate root and crown observations.

title: Spotted Cucumber Beetle
organization: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management
authors: Utah State University Extension Integrated Pest Management Program
supportedClaims: Utah hemp guidance describes adults as ovoid yellow-green beetles with a black head, legs, antennae, and 12 black wing spots; listed look-alikes include western and northern corn rootworms and other yellow-and-black chrysomelids.
On hemp, the damaging life stage is the adult, which chews irregular holes in leaves; damage is characterized as minor and adults can also be scouted on stems and flowers.
The guide explicitly states that soil larvae are not known to feed on hemp roots, conflicting with a Missouri Extension statement that larvae can feed on hemp root hairs and tips.
The reported Utah seasonality, low threat rating, and numeric treatment trigger are regional guidance rather than validated universal Cannabis thresholds.

title: Thrips
organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Onion thrips and western flower thrips occur on field- and greenhouse-grown hemp; adults are minute, elongated, yellow to yellow-brown insects with fringed wings and larvae are creamy yellow and wingless.
Feeding on hemp produces white flecks or silvery scars with dark fecal spots, often along veins, and feeding on developing leaves can distort them.
Field injury is usually minor in Utah, economic damage is more likely indoors, and no industrial-hemp treatment threshold is established.
The two hemp symptom photographs on the page are credited collectively to the USU Extension IPM Program, while the page provides no explicit reuse license.

title: Documentation of Boron Deficiency and Phytotoxicity in Cannabis sativa to Aid in Development of the GrowDoc Application
organization: Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre, Niagara College
publisher: Niagara College Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre
supportedClaims: Three White Shark Cannabis clones per treatment were grown in deep-water culture with 0.0063 mM boron control solution, zero-boron solution, or 0.05 mM boron toxicity solution; pH and EC were monitored and mature leaf tissue was analyzed by an external laboratory.

The 0.05 mM treatment developed marginal chlorosis within three weeks, quickly followed by bronze necrosis; the injury occurred on both upper and lower leaves and affected nearly every leaf in the three treated plants.
The boron-toxicity tissue analysis was elevated while other measured nutrients were described as sufficient, strengthening the treatment-to-symptom link under this small controlled trial.

In this trial, toxicity caused persistent leaf-margin injury but height, SPAD, yield, and measured THC remained close to controls, showing that visual severity must not be converted into a universal yield-loss estimate.

Researchers captured weekly close-ups, whole-plant photographs, and 360-degree video, but the public report does not expose original video asset URLs or a reuse license; those unlinked assets cannot be admitted to this dataset.

title: Spider Mites
organization: University of California Statewide IPM Program
publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
supportedClaims: Spider-mite feeding can cause stippling, bronzing or yellowing, leaf drop, and fine silk webbing; damage can remain visible after mites have left, so injury alone does not establish an active infestation.

Diagnosis should include leaf-underside inspection with a hand lens and tapping suspect foliage over white paper to look for moving mites; eggs, mites, and webbing provide stronger evidence than leaf color alone.
Predatory mites are typically more active and have longer legs than plant-feeding spider mites, so visible mite-like organisms are not automatically pests.

title: An adult Japanese beetle, Popillia japonica
organization: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program
publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
supportedClaims: Twelve discrete patches of short white hairs around the abdomen distinguish adult Japanese beetle from similar-looking beetles.
The institutional specimen image is credited to Clemson University–USDA Cooperative Extension Slide Series, Bugwood.org, and is licensed CC BY 3.0 US.

title: Foliar Diseases of Outdoor Hemp (Cannabis sativa) and Their Management 2021
publisher: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs
supportedClaims: In Ontario field hemp, downy mildew risk increased as canopies closed, humidity accumulated in the canopy center, and extended leaf wetness occurred.
Symptoms began as small reddish-brown irregular spots with irregular yellow halos, expanded into roughly circular patches, and became elongated and confined by leaf veins.

Purplish-gray fuzz could appear on the lower surface beneath lesions in the morning and disappear after spores dispersed in the first winds of the day, making capture time a critical negative-evidence limitation.
Unlike Septoria lesions, the documented downy-mildew lesions lacked black pycnidia; unlike powdery mildew, the causal organism is an oomycete rather than a surface-growing fungus.

Figures 4 and 5 are Cannabis symptom photographs credited to Amy Fang Shi, OGGA, but the page states no reusable image or automated-training license; they are indexed only as rights-restricted reference metadata.

title: Exserohilum Leaf Spot Causing Problems in NC Hemp
supportedClaims: NC State Extension identifies Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot on multiple industrial-hemp strains in North Carolina and warns that other hemp leaf spots can look similar, so accurate diagnosis is important.
The institutional hemp description states that Exserohilum can affect leaves, stems, and flowers; leaf lesions are most distinct as small round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers.
As lesions age, spores may appear in gray-brown centers like fine ground pepper and lesions may coalesce into larger irregular necrotic areas; these are progression cues, not species confirmation.
The page names bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as similar hemp diseases and characterizes bacterial leaf spot/blight as angular, supporting explicit differential checks.

NC State Extension states that hemp leaf spots can look similar and accurate diagnosis is important; its industrial-hemp bacterial leaf spot/blight reference is characterized only as angular lesions and is not presented as species-confirmed Serratia ground truth.

The same institutional differential describes Exserohilum lesions as small, round spots with dark-brown margins and gray-brown centers that may develop pepper-like spores as they age, helping separate a fungal leaf-spot pattern from vein-limited bacterial-compatible injury.
The page identifies bacterial, Fusarium, and Septoria leaf spots as visual alternatives to Exserohilum, supporting a multi-pathogen differential rather than an image-only bacterial species label.

title: Hemp-Cucumber beetle
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: The Pacific Northwest hemp guide describes the western spotted cucumber beetle as yellowish green, approximately 0.25 inch long, and bearing 11 black spots on the wing covers.
Adults eat small holes in leaves and flowers and are commonly found feeding on hemp.
Damage to mature hemp is usually minor, and the regional guide states that scouting thresholds are unnecessary because it treats the beetle as a minor hemp pest.
This western regional description and management conclusion must not be generalized to other subspecies, seedling stages, climates, or production systems.

title: Hemp-Lygus bug
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: The regional hemp profile includes Lygus hesperus, Lygus elisus, and Lygus lineolaris and cautions that Lygus hesperus and Lygus elisus are the most common PNW species.
Adults are 4.4 to 6.3 mm long, range from light green to brown or black, and bear a V-shaped or triangular scutellar mark; nymphs are green or yellow-green with black dorsal spots.
In the Pacific Northwest, Lygus can occur throughout the hemp growing season and higher counts may occur from late July to mid-August near flowering; this timing is regional rather than universal.
Beating sheets or trays, vacuum sampling, and direct observation can recover mixed adult and nymph stages, while no hemp treatment threshold or established economic-damage relationship exists.
Alfalfa, quinoa, weeds, and other hosts may produce populations that later colonize hemp, so nearby-host context and field distribution should be recorded.

title: Greenhouse ornamental—Fungus gnat
supportedClaims: Institutional greenhouse guidance describes fungus-gnat larvae as small, white, legless maggots with black head capsules and adults as delicate, black-bodied flies with long legs and antennae.
A Y-shaped wing vein helps distinguish adult fungus gnats from shore flies, which are stouter, have short antennae, and have five white wing spots.

Larvae feed on decaying material and roots, high populations can kill seedlings, and both larvae and adults may move pathogen spores; these cross-crop statements do not prove Cannabis injury in a particular image.
Yellow sticky cards can monitor adults, potato pieces can monitor larvae, and roots of poorly performing plants should be inspected directly; wet conditions and poor drainage favor populations.
The page gives greenhouse life-stage timings, but those values are context-dependent cross-crop guidance and must not be treated as universal Cannabis progression intervals.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Brown Blight (Alternaria Diseases)
organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: Alternaria alternata and potentially other Alternaria species can infect Cannabis leaves, petioles, stems, and flower parts; infected crop and weed residue can produce conidia that move by wind and water.

Compatible Cannabis symptoms include small dark or yellow leaf spots that enlarge into brown-to-gray circular lesions, sometimes with concentric rings, dark borders, yellow halos, or sooty black spore masses in lesion centers.
Cannabis leaves and buds can begin brown and darken toward brown-black as sporulation develops; these organ and temporal observations are compatible signs, not species confirmation.
OSU surveys in 2021 observed hemp leaf spots about 0.1 inch or smaller, while higher relative humidity can be associated with larger spots; lesion size is therefore context-dependent.
The institutional guidance emphasizes improving air circulation, minimizing leaf wetness, and removing infected leaves; these are risk-reduction measures and do not substitute for diagnosis.
The page is institutionally copyrighted and exposes no explicit reusable license for disease media; no page graphic was copied or indexed as training ground truth.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Cercospora Leaf Spot (Olive Leaf Spot)
organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: The institutional handbook lists both Cercospora cannabis and Pseudocercospora cannabina as Cannabis olive-leaf-spot causes that can overwinter on infected crop residue at the soil surface.

Olive leaf spot is reported more commonly in field-grown hemp; greenhouse observations are most common near open doors or vents, making location and exposure context useful but non-confirmatory metadata.
Pseudocercospora cannabina can cause complete defoliation, while the page distinguishes the gray-centered, dark-bordered circular-to-elliptical spots described for Cercospora cannabis.
The handbook recommends improving air circulation, minimizing leaf wetness, and removing infected leaves as cultural risk-reduction measures; these practices do not establish the causal species.
The institutional page does not provide an item-level reusable Pseudocercospora image license, so no page media were copied or indexed for training.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Curly Top
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Hemp curly-top symptoms vary with variety, growth stage, temperature, and virus strain; predominant signs include stunting, twisted or curled leaves, and pale-green-to-yellow foliage.
Leaves may pucker and curl upward, or remain green while new growth twists and stem growth is stunted; earlier infection generally produces more severe symptoms.
Individual plants can contain symptomatic and apparently healthy shoot portions or appear to outgrow visible symptoms.
The four hemp symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2021; the landing page states copyright but provides no reuse license.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Gray Mold (Botrytis Bud Blight and Stem Canker)
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: Gray mold can affect Cannabis seedlings, stems, foliage, and flowers; brown water-soaked bud spots can progress to dead inflorescences covered by brown to gray-brown spores.
Stem infection can produce cankers, splitting or breakage, and black sclerotia, while heavily affected plants can decline quickly under conducive conditions.
Cool, humid or wet conditions and prolonged tissue wetness favor disease, but environmental conditions are risk context rather than proof of cause.

The page photographs show a close exterior bud-rot view, a close sporulating-flower view, and a whole-plant distribution view; each is credited to Cynthia M. Ocamb in 2020, and the page states copyright without an explicit media-reuse license.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Rhizoctonia Soreshin and Root Rot
organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
authors: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: The March 2026 institutional revision identifies Rhizoctonia solani as the cause, states that it can persist in soil for at least several years, has a broad host range, and can spread with infected plant debris.
The hemp description records dry brown root rot and reddish-brown rot on the lower main stem; it also reports dry brown leaf tissue and bud infection in Oregon medical Cannabis.

Warmer soil favors disease, while early over-irrigation and irrigation-related soil cooling can slow emergence and favor the fungus; these conditions are epidemiologic context and are not diagnostic proof.

The handbook recommends rotation away from susceptible hosts and avoiding early over-irrigation, supporting soil/debris movement and irrigation-history checks without establishing a universal treatment interval for every production system.

title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Witches’ Broom
publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: Cannabis witches’ broom expression varies with the phytoplasma involved; typical plants are stunted with highly branched stems, axillary shoot proliferation, and small, distorted, chlorotic leaves.
Phytoplasmas are leafhopper-transmitted, regional pathogen types vary, and vector presence or symptoms alone do not identify the phytoplasma involved.
The three cannabis symptom photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb, Oregon State University, 2022; the landing page states copyright but supplies no reuse license.

title: Cabbage Looper
publisher: Virginia Tech and Virginia State University
supportedClaims: Cross-crop identification guidance describes cabbage looper larvae as pale green, relatively smooth, thinly white-striped caterpillars that arch or loop while crawling and can reach approximately 1.5 inches long.

Two pairs of abdominal prolegs on abdominal segments five and six help distinguish cabbage looper larvae from imported cabbageworm larvae, which have four pairs; incomplete or obscured ventral views cannot support that exclusion.
In non-Cannabis crops, early instars feed from leaf undersides and may leave the opposite epidermis intact, while later instars chew through leaves and sticky frass can occur near feeding sites.
Virginia cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower thresholds are crop-specific and must not be transferred to Cannabis or hemp.

title: Broad Mite
supportedClaims: Broad mites prefer young, protected tissue and may no longer be present on the most damaged tissue because visible injury can persist after feeding.
Clear oval broad-mite eggs have raised pale dots, while cyclamen-mite eggs are smooth and russet mites have a narrow, conical body form.
Broad-mite injury can resemble plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury, nutrient problems, and other abiotic disorders; inspection at about 20× or by microscope is recommended.

title: Sampling for Plant Tissue Analysis
organization: New Mexico State University Extension, Guide A-123
publisher: New Mexico State University College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences
supportedClaims: Plant tissue analysis can detect nutrient deficiencies before visible symptoms occur and can help confirm suspected visual deficiencies; abnormal appearance alone does not establish a nutrient cause.

Diagnostic sampling should compare physiologically similar abnormal and normal plants from the same area, exclude unrelated pest, disease, moisture, and mechanical stress, and retain crop, variety, fertilizer, irrigation, appearance, insect, and disease context for interpretation.

Where crop-specific instructions are unavailable, the guide recommends recently mature leaves below the growing point from multiple plants and warns that residues, unsuitable leaf age, diseased tissue, poor handling, and unmatched single plants can invalidate interpretation.
The guide includes molybdenum among elements available by tissue analysis but does not provide a Cannabis-specific sufficiency or deficiency threshold.

title: Hemp Disease and Pest Management
supportedClaims: University of Tennessee Extension reports fungus-gnat larvae as a root-feeding pest of hemp grown under greenhouse conditions and states that they may increase root-disease incidence.

The guide also states that much remains unknown about arthropod pests in hemp; its report supports a greenhouse-hemp association but not a universal symptom, damage threshold, species label, or causal attribution from an adult capture alone.

title: Herbicide Damage Symptoms on Hemp
organization: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, UC Weed Science
publisher: Regents of the University of California
supportedClaims: The institutional hemp demonstration exposed plants to herbicides used near hemp production to document injury expected from specific active ingredients or related modes of action.

Its clomazone example identifies carotenoid-biosynthesis inhibition: bleaching ranges from yellow to almost pure white, begins in newly formed tissue, may progress to older tissue as existing carotenoids turn over, and can advance to necrosis.

The guide distinguishes potentially dramatic but rarely lethal established-plant drift injury from more damaging soil-carryover injury to seedlings or young transplants; these are contextual patterns, not dose-independent outcome guarantees.

The source PDF contains mixed herbicide-treatment photographs without a verified reusable asset license or panel-level training labels, so those figures are citation evidence only and are not indexed as reusable media.

title: Pathogen Safety Data Sheets: Infectious Substances – Serratia spp.
authors: Pathogen Regulation Directorate, Public Health Agency of Canada
supportedClaims: The Public Health Agency of Canada identifies Serratia species as Gram-negative rods and notes that many, but not all, species or strains produce a red-to-pink pigment; pigment therefore cannot be required for or used alone as species confirmation.

The agency describes Serratia species as opportunistic pathogens, classifies the genus as Risk Group 2 while noting that the classification may not apply to every species, and specifies Containment Level 2 practices for potentially infectious material or cultures.

For work with infected material or cultures, the sheet calls for protective clothing, gloves where direct contact is unavoidable, eye protection where splashes are possible, and controls for aerosol-producing procedures.
